I want to write about dust.

Not metaphorical dust. Real dust.

The kind that hangs in a sunbeam in the late afternoon, when the light comes through a window at just the right angle and the air itself becomes visible. Most of the time we pretend air is empty. Transparent. Nothing. But then the light hits it a certain way and you see that it's completely full - of skin cells and pollen and bits of fabric and soil lifted from a field a thousand miles away and probably a little bit of you that you breathed out earlier.

Dust is a kind of memory. Everything that has happened in a room leaves a trace of itself floating there. If you never dusted your bookshelf, archaeologists of the future could reconstruct your life: what sweater you wore, what plant flowered on your windowsill in April, what bread you toasted.

And I love that it never settles forever. You wipe it away, and it comes back. You vacuum, you sweep, you filter the air, and a day later the sunbeam is full again. It's not dirtiness, exactly. It's just the world refusing to sit still. Things rubbing against things, breaking into smaller things, traveling.

Humans tend to think in categories - inside and outside, mine and yours, past and present. Dust ignores all of that. The Sahara Desert ends up on cars in Paris. Volcanic ash from Iceland ends up in lungs in Scotland. Dead stars end up in your bones and then, inevitably, in your living room.

There's a quiet comfort in that, I think. The idea that even when a room is still and quiet and empty, it's still exchanging pieces of itself with the rest of the planet. Nothing is truly sealed off.

Maybe that's why I like libraries and attics and old shops - places where dust is allowed to exist. They feel more honest than sterile, wiped-clean spaces. They admit that time has passed here. That people have been here, and left, and will come back.

If you have a moment today where the sun comes in low and gold, watch the dust for 30 seconds. Don't think of it as something to clean.

Think of it as the air finally letting you see it breathe.
